content:
Apple has submitted its proposal regarding the fee amount for transactions outside the App Store system in the Epic Games case. Details are as follows.

Apple submits proposal for App Store external transaction commission

After numerous attempts to halt proceedings in federal district court to determine how much Apple may charge (if anything) for transactions outside its App Store in-app purchase (IAP) system, Apple has finally submitted its proposal, outlining the suggested fee structure.

Apple's submission comes as the U.S. Supreme Court denied Apple's request to halt proceedings in the lower court. Apple had previously applied to the Supreme Court for a stay of execution, hoping to suspend related proceedings while the Supreme Court reviewed a case alleging Apple violated a court order by charging a 27% commission on App Store external transactions. Previously, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers had issued an injunction requiring Apple to allow developers to steer users to alternative payment methods.

Apple had argued in both the lower court and subsequently at the Supreme Court that the court's ruling could affect the outcome of the proceedings to determine the fee amount, and that related proceedings should therefore be suspended before the court reaches a decision. However, the Supreme Court denied Apple's application, allowing the lower court proceedings to continue while the Supreme Court conducts its review.

As a result, Apple has now submitted its proposal, which is as follows:

Standard apps charged at 15% (originally subject to the 30% in-app purchase commission); Video Partner Program (VPP), News Partner Program (NPP), Mini Apps Partner Program (MPP), and subscription renewals at 10%; apps under the Small Business Program at 5%.

Apple stated: "The factual and expert evidence supporting these proposed commission rates has been submitted together." The company added:

Apple also noted that its "proposed external link commission can also be compared with commissions charged by other app stores competing with the App Store," including Google Play, Samsung Galaxy Store, and Amazon's Android App Marketplace.

The company also mentioned that "Google Play Store's external link rates are 20% for standard, 15% for partner programs, and 10% for subscriptions, and Epic has agreed to these rates."

Apple stated it still believes that the proceedings to determine the fee rate should be suspended while the case is pending at the Supreme Court, and that this submission of its proposal is solely to comply with Judge Gonzalez Rogers's instructions.

The company also mentioned that the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals has overturned the district court's ruling that completely prohibited charging commissions on external link transactions, noting that an issue would only arise if the commission was actually intimidating in nature.

With the proposal submitted, Epic will have an opportunity to respond, and Apple is expected to file its brief with the Supreme Court by September 14.
